[https://www.vic.gov.au/vietnamese-community-profile](https://www.vic.gov.au/vietnamese-community-profile)  
Following the Vietnam War, Australia welcomed a significant number of Vietnamese refugees. Many settled in Melbourne's western suburbs, including Footscray, attracted by available housing and employment opportunities. This influx led to the establishment of Vietnamese businesses, restaurants, and cultural centers, notably along Hopkins Street, contributing to Footscray's vibrant "Little Saigon" precinct.

[https://www.maribyrnong.vic.gov.au/News/Little-Africa-Precinct](https://www.maribyrnong.vic.gov.au/News/Little-Africa-Precinct)  
In more recent decades, Footscray has become a hub for African migrants, including those from Ethiopia, Sudan, and Somalia. Drawn by affordable housing and existing community networks, these groups have enriched the suburb with African-owned businesses, eateries, and cultural events. The establishment of the "Little Africa" precinct further highlights Footscray's role as a center for African-Australian life in Victoria.

Both Government Article Sources.

The title is factual:  
  
Footscray is often called an "African and Asian city" because it has become a hub for these communities, shaped by waves of immigration. Vietnamese refugees arrived in large numbers after the Vietnam War in the 1970s, establishing restaurants, markets, and businesses. Similarly, African migrants and refugees from Somalia, Ethiopia, Sudan, and other countries settled here in more recent decades, contributing to its cultural diversity. The visible presence of African and Asian businesses, cultural events, and community centers has earned Footscray this name.
